doc.title: Frank Foster — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Outside Basie: Monk, Coltrane, Elvin Jones
title: Writing for Elvin's group versus Basie
summary: With Elvin he wrote melodies and small-group lines rather than section figures.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Did you find there a venue for you to not only play differently, but compose differently, for some of your harmonic ideas to be more fully heard?

Oh, yes. It was a totally different avenue, approach. I thought in a more contemporary fashion, in less of a big-band format. Everything I composed for Basie had to be thought of in the context of a big band with figures, trumpet-section figures, saxophone-section figures. I didn’t have to think like that writing for Elvin. All I had to do was think of melodies, linear statements. Of course there was always the harmonic structure that had to go in there, but these were melodies of a more contemporary nature.
But you could also think of exploring rhythms, and in this case the holes weren’t for clink, clink, clink, but they were for thunder.
Any other combinations of instruments, you playing other things besides tenor?

I had the E-flat alto clarinet. Most people thought it was a bass clarinet. It’s similar to a bass clarinet, only it’s smaller. But there weren’t too many other instruments involved. There might be another tenor saxophonist, and soprano sax or a flute involved, but the writing was much smaller than for the Basie orchestra, but much more contemporary.
